result.summary: After the flood, Deucalion and Pyrrha go weeping to the temple of Themis to ask how mankind can be restored. The oracle tells them to throw their great mother's bones behind them, and Deucalion works out that these are stones. The thrown stones become men and women, which is why humans are hardy.

scenes.title: Prayer at Themis's temple
scenes.summary: Deucalion and Pyrrha weep, wash in the Cephisus and go to the neglected temple. There they prostrate themselves and ask Themis how to restore their race.
scenes.stakes: The whole human race has been lost; they must find a way to renew it or be the last survivors.

place.name: Temple of Themis by the Cephisus

scenes.title: The riddling oracle
scenes.summary: Themis tells them to cover their heads, loosen their garments and throw their mother's bones behind them. Pyrrha refuses at first, and Deucalion reasons that the bones are stones.
scenes.stakes: Pyrrha fears offending her mother's shade; both risk misreading the oracle and committing sacrilege.

place.name: Temple of Themis by the Cephisus

scenes.title: Stones become people
scenes.summary: They cast stones behind them, and the stones soften and take human shape. Those thrown by the man become men and those thrown by the woman become women, and the poet says humans show their stony origin.
scenes.stakes: The survival of humanity depends on the oracle's command being fulfilled.

notable_quotes.reason: The oracle's famous riddle: throw the bones of your great mother behind you.
Ovid's closing explanation of humanity's toughness through its stony origin.

analysis.text: The passage shows renewal after destruction, with piety and clever interpretation of divine commands rewarded by the recreation of mankind.
It is an aetiological myth that explains human endurance and perhaps a Greek pun, since laos means people and laas means stone.

legacy.text: The Deucalion and Pyrrha flood story became a standard classical parallel to Noah's flood and was often retold in later European art and literature.

fun_facts.text: The wordplay linking stones and people works in Greek (laas and laos), though Ovid writes in Latin, where lapis and populus do not rhyme.

language_notes.text: Cephisus is a river in Phocis and Boeotia. It is 'not yet clear' because the flood has only just subsided, leaving it muddy, though back in its usual bed.
Sprinkling water on clothes and heads is a ritual purification before approaching a god's shrine.
Covering the head and loosening the girdle are ritual acts of reverence and humility. 'Great mother' is deliberately ambiguous, which creates the riddle.
Deucalion is the son of Prometheus, who made humans from clay, and Pyrrha is the daughter of Epimetheus, Prometheus's brother.
Pyrrha is 'descended from Titan' because her father Epimetheus was a son of the Titan Iapetus. The note's footnote refers to this Titan lineage.
The 'same name' is a wordplay: Latin 'vena' means a vein of blood and also a vein in stone or ore.

context_notes.text: Themis is the Titan goddess of divine law and order. She held an oracle, and in Ovid she is the one who advises the survivors of the flood.
Her temple is ruined and unkept because the flood has wiped out worshippers. The neglected state underlines how total the destruction was.

literary_notes.text: Pyrrha's fear of offending her mother's shade shows her piety and caution, in contrast with Deucalion's reasoning.
The narrator interrupts to admit the story is hard to believe, appealing to ancient tradition as proof. This gives the poet's voice a note of ironic distance.
The half-formed people are compared to rough marble statues, showing the stage between stone and flesh.
The poet ends by explaining a human trait, endurance, as inherited from the stones. The narrator turns to 'we', linking myth to the present.
